title: Burst sway: latency vs $/k-token brief
summary: Short working note. Purpose: capture experimental results for burst-oscillation behavior ("sway") and its dollar impact across three candidate serving configurations. This is a lightweight field report for product & SRE planning; not final. Key takeaway (tentative): some quantization+prefetch combos reduce $/k-token while slightly widening p99 under heavy oscillation; fallback stitching reduces cost but increases median latency in microbursts.
methodology:
Test harness: replayed production-like arrival traces (06:00–07:00 PDT weekday microburst window) driven from traffic-simulator v0.9. Configs tested in parallel on identical hardware (A100-sim nodes):
- cfg-A: baseline dense FP16 model (full KV cache, conservative batching)
- cfg-B: q4_0 quantized model with aggressive packing + small-session tiling
- cfg-C: hybrid-stitch (small model fastpath + async stitching to large model on miss)
Each run: 1 hour, 10 warmup minutes discarded. Measured: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms), throughput (qps), effective cost ($/k-token) using internal cost model (GPU time + EC2 networking). Notes: arrival trace contains repeating oscillation patterns at 5–15s cadence (sway).
results:
Aggregated metrics (median of 3 runs):

Table (numbers approximate):
cfg | p50 ms | p90 ms | p99 ms | throughput qps | $/k-token
----|--------|--------|--------|---------------|---------
cfg-A | 48 | 122 | 410 | 860 | 0.54
cfg-B | 62 | 160 | 620 | 1210 | 0.38
cfg-C | 85 | 210 | 980 | 720 | 0.29

Observations: cfg-B reduces dollar cost by ~30% vs cfg-A while raising p99 by ~50–60%. cfg-C yields lowest $/k-token (stitching amortizes expensive layers) but increases p50 and p90 noticeably during sway spikes; p99 is worst-case due to miss amplification and stitching tail. Throughput tradeoffs: cfg-B packs more tokens and achieves higher steady qps but suffers larger p99 under brief large-concurrency oscillations.

conclusions:
- If goal is predictable p99 SLOs for interactive features, cfg-A (baseline) is simplest despite higher $/k-token.
- For cost-conscious workloads tolerant of p99 variance, cfg-B (quantized+packing) is a strong sweet spot.
- cfg-C (stitch) is attractive where median cost matters (batching/embeddings pipelines) but needs tighter miss-rate controls and prefetch heuristics before adopting for low-latency user-facing paths.
- Important: oscillatory patterns (sway) disproportionately affect any aggressive packing/tiling strategy due to sudden shifts in concurrency and KV cache validity; operator tooling should surface an "oscillation index" and recommend fallbacks when index > threshold.
